question: Did Jesus have a human soul and mind, or did the Word replace them?
search: what is not assumed is not healed

answers.label: He had a full human soul and mind
The divine Word took the place of a human mind

overview.text: Apollinaris of Laodicea, about 375, taught that in Christ the divine Word took the place of a human mind, so that Christ was "mind made flesh".

A synod at Alexandria in 362 had already said the Savior's body was not without soul or mind. Gregory of Nazianzus answered with the rule that what Christ did not take on, he did not heal: the whole of Adam fell, so the whole was assumed.

quotes.author: Origen of Alexandria
quotes.english: With this substance of a soul, then, mediating between God and flesh (for it was not possible for the nature of God to be mingled with a body without a mediator), there is born, as we have said, the God-man, that mediating substance being present, for which it was not contrary to nature to take a body. ... that there is a rational soul in Christ, we have shown above. ... The nature of that soul was the same as the nature of all souls; this cannot be doubted, for otherwise it could not even be called a soul, if it was not truly a soul.
quotes.original: Hac ergo substantia animae inter Deum carnemque mediante, non enim possibile erat Dei naturam corpori sine mediatore misceri, nascitur, ut diximus, Deus homo, illa substantia media exsistente, cui utique contra naturam non erat corpus assumere. ... rationabilem animam esse in Christo supra ostendimus ... Naturam quidem animae illius hanc fuisse, quae est omnium animarum, non potest dubitari: alioquin nec dici anima potuit, si vere non fuit anima.
quotes.context: Origen's account of the incarnation, a century and a half before Apollinaris: Christ's soul, clinging inseparably to the Word from the beginning, is the mediator by which the Word is joined to flesh, and it is a true rational soul of the same nature as every soul. On First Principles survives in full mainly in Rufinus's Latin translation, which sometimes smooths Origen; the passage is read here in that Latin.

source.edition: Lommatzsch, Origenis opera omnia, vol. 21 (1847), De principiis 2.6.3–5

quotes.author: Athanasius of Alexandria (council of Alexandria)
quotes.english: They also confessed this: that the Savior did not have a body without soul, or without sense, or without mind. For it was not possible, when the Lord became man for us, that his body should be without mind; nor was it the body alone but the soul too that found salvation in the Word himself.
quotes.original: Ὡμολόγουν γὰρ καὶ τοῦτο, ὅτι οὐ σῶμα ἄψυχον, οὐδ' ἀναίσθητον, οὐδ' ἀνόητον εἶχεν ὁ Σωτήρ. Οὐδὲ γὰρ οἷόν τε ἦν, τοῦ Κυρίου δι' ἡμᾶς ἀνθρώπου γενομένου, ἀνόητον εἶναι τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ, οὐδὲ σώματος μόνου, ἀλλὰ καὶ ψυχῆς ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ Λόγῳ σωτηρία γέγονεν
quotes.context: A synod at Alexandria in 362 settles the question before it becomes a schism.

quotes.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea (quoted by Gregory of Nyssa)
quotes.english: He would not have come in the likeness of man unless, like a man, he were mind made flesh. ... If the Lord is not mind made flesh, he would be wisdom enlightening a human mind. But that is in all people. And if so, Christ's coming was not God's coming to live among us, but a man's birth.
quotes.original: οὐ γὰρ ἄν (φησιν) ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπου γεγονὼς εἴη, εἰ μὴ τυγχάνοι καθάπερ ἄνθρωπος νοῦς ἔνσαρκος ὦν. ... εἰ μὴ νοῦς ἔνσαρκός ἐστιν ὁ κύριος, σοφία ἂν εἴη φωτίζουσα νοῦν ἀνθρώπου. αὕτη δὲ καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις· εἰ δὲ ταῦτα, οὐκ ἦν ἐπιδημία θεοῦ ἡ Χριστοῦ παρουσία, ἀλλ᾽ ἀνθρώπου γέννησις.
quotes.context: Apollinaris, once Athanasius's ally, held that the divine Word took the place of a human mind in Christ, to keep Christ one and sinless.

source.edition: Lietzmann, Apollinaris von Laodicea und seine Schule (1904), fragments 69–70, from Gregory of Nyssa's Antirrheticus

quotes.author: Council of Constantinople
quotes.english: that every heresy should be anathematized, and in particular that of the Eunomians, that is, the Anomoeans, and that of the Arians, that is, the Eudoxians, and that of the Semi-Arians, that is, the Pneumatomachians, and that of the Sabellians, and that of the Marcellians, and that of the Photinians, and that of the Apollinarians.
quotes.original: ἀναθεματισθῆναι πᾶσαν αἵρεσιν, καὶ ἰδικῶς τὴν τῶν Εὐνομιανῶν, εἴτουν Ἀνομοίων, καὶ τὴν τῶν Ἀρειανῶν, εἴτουν Εὐδοξιανῶν, καὶ τὴν τῶν Ἡμιαρειανῶν, εἴτουν Πνευματομάχων, καὶ τὴν τῶν Σαβελλιανῶν, καὶ τὴν τῶν Μαρκελλιανῶν, καὶ τὴν τῶν Φωτεινιανῶν, καὶ τὴν τῶν Ἀπολλιναριστῶν.
quotes.context: The first canon of Constantinople (381) first confirms the faith of Nicaea and then names the condemned teachings one by one. Apollinaris, who made the Word take the place of Christ's human mind, is named in the council's own anathema.

source.edition: Bright, The Canons of the First Four General Councils (2nd ed., Oxford, 1892), Greek text

quotes.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
quotes.english: If anyone has put his hope in a man without a mind, he is truly mindless himself and unworthy of salvation. For what was not assumed was not healed; but what is united to God is saved. If half of Adam fell, then half was assumed and half is saved; but if the whole of Adam fell, the whole is united to the one who was born, and the whole is saved.
quotes.original: Εἴ τις εἰς ἄνουν ἄνθρωπον ἤλπικεν, ἀνόητος ὄντως ἐστὶ καὶ οὐκ ἄξιος ὅλως σῴζεσθαι. Τὸ γὰρ ἀπρόσληπτον, ἀθεράπευτον· ὃ δὲ ἥνωται τῷ Θεῷ, τοῦτο καὶ σῴζεται. Εἰ ἥμισυς ἔπταισεν ὁ Ἀδάμ, ἥμισυ καὶ τὸ προσειλημμένον καὶ τὸ σῳζόμενον. Εἰ δὲ ὅλος, ὅλῳ τῷ γεννηθέντι ἥνωται καὶ ὅλως σῴζεται.
quotes.context: "What was not assumed was not healed": the most quoted line against Apollinaris. Constantinople (381) condemned his teaching.

method: Every early quote was read in its Greek or Latin and translated for this page by Claude (Opus 5.5) on 13 October 2026. Each line names the printed edition it was read from.
